::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Calculating the odds of winning a card game](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/635379/calculating-the-odds-of-winning-a-card-game), asked by [Lex](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/120733/lex) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2014-01-12; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> So my friend made this game and I want to the odds of winning his game. So his game is basically I pay \$$1$ to draw $2$ cards from the deck and guess $2$ numbers and one suit. For each correct guess I get \$$1$. Doubled guesses still only count for one correct guess. So either I lose \$$1$($0$correct guess), break even ($1$correct guess), profit \$$1$($2$correct guesses) or profit \$$2$($3$ correct guesses).
>
> To win, I have to profit at least \$$1$ so that means I need to be able to guess either both numbers, or one number and one suit.
>
> I was wondering what my odds of winning are or what the odds of all possibilities are.
:::

This is a fun game! But don't play it.

Based on what you wrote twelve years ago, here's how I assume the game works:

* Two random cards are dealt from a standard deck, face down.
* You guess two ranks (the “number” on the card) and one suit.
* You get a dollar if your first rank matches one of the cards, a dollar if your second rank matches one of the cards, and a dollar if your suit matches one of the cards.

I'm inferring this from your sentence “Doubled guesses still only count for one correct guess” and that the set of payoff outcomes is $\{0,1,2,3\}$. If two cards of the same suit, guessed correctly, count for \$2, then you could get \$4 if you guessed both ranks and the shared suit correctly. I'm also assuming that you wouldn't guess the same rank twice; that would seem to be a wasted guess if “doubled guesses still only count for one correct guess.”

Let's name some events and random variables:

* Let $R_1$, $R_2$, $S_1$, and $S_2$ be the rank and suit of the two cards dealt. These are categorical [random variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_variable), which we assume uniformly distributed among the possible values (i.e., the deck is fair).
* Let $G_1$, $G_2$, and $G_3$ be the two ranks and suit guessed. 
* Let $W_1$, $W_2$, and $W_3$ be the events that your two ranks and suit match the cards dealt.
* Let $X_1$, $X_2$, and $X_3$ be the dollar amounts you get from the ranks and suit matching. These are numerical random variables.

You asked for $P(W_1)$, $P(W_2)$, and $P(W_3)$ (the probabilities of winning in each way), and also $E(X_1+X_2+X_3)$ (the [expected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value) winnings per game).

Let's calculate:
$$\begin{aligned}
P(W_1) &= P((G_1 = R_1) \cup (G_1 = R_2))
\\&= P(G_1 = R_1) + P(G_1 = R_2) - P((G_1 = R_1) \cap (G_1 = R_2))
\end{aligned}$$

There are $13$ possible ranks, so it's pretty clear that $P(G_1 = R_1) = \frac{1}{13}$. It's also true that $P(G_1 = R_2) = \frac{1}{13}$. People find this hard to believe, because $R_1$ and $R_2$ are dependent on each other. But you can convince yourself two ways:

* Either calculate it carefully conditioning on the rank of the first card:
$$P(G_1 = R_2) = P(G_1 = R_2 \mid G_1 = R_1)P(G_1 = R_1) + P(G_1 = R_2 \mid G_1 \neq R_1)P(G_1 \neq R_1)$$
* Or just imagine swapping the two cards dealt before turning them face up, or dealing them right-to-left instead of left-to-right. The set of outcomes isn't changed, so the probabilities wouldn't change.

As for $P((G_1 = R_1) \cap (G_1 = R_2))$, there are $\binom{52}{2}$ ways to choose two cards, and $\binom{4}{2}$ ways to choose two cards of a fixed rank (since there are four cards of the same rank in the deck). 
So
$$P((G_1 = R_1) \cap (G_1 = R_2))
= \frac{\binom{4}{2}}{\binom{52}{2}} = \frac{4 \cdot 3}{52 \cdot 51} = \frac{1}{13 \cdot 17}$$
and finally
$$P(W_1) = \frac{1}{13} + \frac{1}{13} - \frac{1}{13 \cdot 17} = \frac{33}{221} \approx 0.149$$

In a similar way, $P(W_2) = P(W_1)$. And using suits instead of ranks, we can compute $P(W_3)$:
$$\begin{aligned}
  P(W_3) &= P(G_3 = S_1) + P(G_3 = S_2) - P(G_3 = S_1 = S_2)
\\&= \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} - \frac{\binom{13}{2}}{\binom{52}{2}}
\\&= \frac{1}{2} - \frac{13 \cdot 12}{52 \cdot 51}
\\&= \frac{45}{102} \approx 0.441
\end{aligned}$$

Now for the payoffs. The rules make it easy, because $X_1$, $X_2$, and $X_3$ payoff \$1 depending on whether $W_1$, $W_2$, or $W_3$ happen. That is:
$$E(X_1) = 1 \cdot P(W_1) + 0 \cdot P(\bar W_1) = P(W_1)$$
and similarly for $X_2$ and $X_3$. Therefore, using the linearity of expectation, we have
$$\begin{aligned}
E(X_1 + X_2 + X_3) &= E(X_1) + E(X_2) + E(X_3)
\\&= P(W_1) + P(W_2) + P(W_3)
\\&= \frac{33}{221} + \frac{33}{221} + \frac{45}{102} \approx 0.740
\end{aligned}$$

I wrote some [python code to simulate this game](https://colab.research.google.com/gist/leingang/27f85555b344bc9441f4e497e7851c6b/lex.ipynb), and the average over a million hands agrees with these calculations.

The [law of large numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_large_numbers) says that, in the limit as the number of iterations grows large, you should expect to win 74 cents per play. If you pay a dollar for each game, you will net an average *loss* of 26 cents per play. So [the only winning move is not to play](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CLJVLwB51LA).
